scope: Local publisher full-text reading of B12, B11, B05 and B06; factual extraction only; no research-route selection. All page numbers are 1-based PDF pages, coinciding with printed article pages.

documents.title: Integrated departure and boundary control for low-altitude air city transport systems
documents.metadata_verification: Title, authors, journal, volume, article number and DOI verified directly on PDF p.1; available online 13 August 2024.

method.control_model: A new accumulation-based control model separates traveling aircraft, ground departure queues and aerial boundary queues. Equations (4)-(8) describe internal/external demand, interregional transfer, boundary-buffer entry and release; states and controls have bounds (14)-(19). The model is written for one-layer multi-region control, with the same modeling methodology intended for multilayer cases and a footnote requiring attention to traffic assignment across layers (pp.6-8, Section 2.4).
method.plant: The microscopic LAAT-Flow plant and macroscopic control model are different. The plant is adopted from Safadi et al. 2023 and uses position/velocity dynamics, bounded speed/acceleration, waypoints and decentralized artificial-potential-field collision avoidance based on Lyapunov-like functions, safety/avoidance/detection spaces (pp.4-5, Sections 2.1-2.2).
method.mfd_identification: Aircraft trajectories are aggregated using generalized Edie definitions to estimate flow/density/speed and regional accumulation/outflow/production. Repeated microscopic simulations identify regional/network airspace states; the unimodal outflow function G(n)=(1/a1)n exp[-(1/a2)(n/a3)^a2] is curve-fitted (pp.5-6, Sections 2.3-2.4).
method.optimization: MPC minimizes weighted squared accumulation plus deviations of departure and boundary control inputs from their reference values; the latter are proxies for departure/boundary delays. At each control step measured plant states initialize the finite-horizon optimization, the first input is applied, then feedback repeats. Direct multiple shooting, Euler discretization, MATLAB R2023b, CasADi and IPOPT implement the controller (pp.7-8, Equations 9-23/Algorithm 1; p.12).
method.macro_to_micro_departure: Algorithm 2 sets delay Delta_td,i=min(max(0,Delta_tC*(1-ud,i)),tf-tk) for queued/inactive aircraft whose departure is in the next control interval, adds the delay to individual departure time and updates individual queue status/index sets (p.9).
method.macro_to_micro_boundary: Boundary input uI determines the ratio allowed to pass; remaining crossing aircraft are assigned a temporary waypoint in a buffer above the region within the same layer and hover. uO determines the ratio discharged. The command system randomly detects aircraft about to cross and applies the queue assignment. Algorithm 3 uses DetBouQueues for counts and ClearToReEnter to check sufficient safety space before reentry (pp.3,9-10; Fig.1/Algorithm 3).
method.actual_feedback: Microscopic trajectory-derived traffic variables and individual states/status/departure times feed the macroscopic model and command subsystem; at each MPC step the current plant accumulation/queues reset initial states. TCPre actuates departure command before aircraft evolution and TCPost actuates boundary command afterward (pp.4-5,8,11,17,19; Fig.2/Algorithms 1,4/Appendix B).
method.time_scales: Microscopic simulation 0.5 s; MFD aggregation 60 s; command/control step 60 s; MPC discretization 60 s, prediction horizon 5 steps (300 s). The general framework requires control step >= MFD estimation interval (pp.8-9,11-12, Table 1).
method.queue_delay_accounting: Control model includes bounded ground departure and aerial boundary queues. Actual performance is TTS=TTT+TDD+TBD, computed directly by summing plant travel time, ground departure delay and boundary delay, rather than treating the quadratic MPC objective as measured TTS (pp.6-8,13,15, Figs.6-9).
method.energy: Energy is a qualitative reason for greater boundary-queue penalties: hovering consumes energy. Objective (13) does not contain a battery/SOC state or a quantified energy cost, and p.15 identifies energy consumption as a separate ongoing study. This is an observed formulation scope, not an author-declared universal limitation (pp.7,12,15).
method.safety: Microscopic APF maintains safety/avoidance spaces and speed saturation; the authors state conflict-free/convergence properties inherited from the model, while ClearToReEnter checks sufficient safety space. The control optimization itself imposes aggregate state/queue/input bounds (pp.5,7-10).

scenario.geometry: Fixed 1.5 km x 1.5 km x 120 m network, city-center region 1 and periphery region 2, no predetermined flight-route structure. Ground origins/destinations are uniform random and aircraft perform VTOL. Fig.3 caption says 'divided into 3 layers'; Section 3.2 says 'two separate layers', with a takeoff/landing layer and a flight layer including a buffer zone. Both descriptions are retained because the PDF does not present them identically (pp.11-12).
scenario.aircraft: Same parameters for every aircraft: maximum speed 20 m/s, acceleration 5 m/s^2, safety radius 15 m, avoidance radius 22.5 m, detection radius 45.5 m (p.11, Table 1 p.12).
scenario.demand_and_comparison: 1 h simulation with trapezoidal demand/warm-up/cool-down. Table 1 lists qm in 0.1..3.7 aircraft/s for airspace identification. Reported NC/DC/BC/DBC comparison uses identical qm=2.5 aircraft/s, versus identified network capacity 2.3 aircraft/s, hence oversaturated. Warm-up ends around 900 s and cooldown starts 2700 s (pp.11-13).
scenario.bounds_and_targets: Region accumulation and corresponding departure/boundary-queue upper bounds are 99 and 405 aircraft; critical accumulations 33 and 135 aircraft; controls bounded [0,1], reference controls 1 (p.12).
scenario.weights: Per-strategy weights are separately calibrated by examining and normalizing objective terms. For DBC wn=0.0004, departure weights 5.4924/22.1800, boundary weights 95.4707; authors connect larger boundary penalties with hovering energy and airspace effects (p.12).

findings.claim: Under the stated oversaturated comparison, DBC maintains stable free flow and has the highest speed profile/outflow. DC avoids gridlock but displays unstable behavior; NC and BC reach congestion/gridlock. Region 2 remains free-flowing; region 1 governs network congestion.

Actual macroscopic control actions are converted into individual departure times and buffer waypoints, with microscopic feedback to the controller. The work therefore demonstrates a concrete macro/micro control loop in simulation.

TTS comparisons include both ground and aerial waiting, not only flight travel time. DBC activates departure control earlier than DC and relaxes during cooldown, whereas DC continues delaying aircraft.

quantitative_findings.result: DC reduces TTS by 32%, BC by 6.7%, and DBC by 40%, each relative to NC.
quantitative_findings.conditions: Same 3D VTOL network, 1 h trapezoid, qm=2.5 aircraft/s > identified Gm=2.3 aircraft/s; separate calibrated MPC weights per strategy.

quantitative_findings.result: Normalized to NC TTS, ground departure-delay share rises from 2.5% (DC) to 4.1% (DBC); DBC adds 0.4% boundary delay and achieves 8 percentage points further TTS reduction relative to the NC-normalized scale.
quantitative_findings.conditions: DC and DBC free-flow cases; percentages in Fig.8 use the same NC TTS denominator and are not within-strategy time shares summing to 100%.

quantitative_findings.result: Critical regional accumulations 33/135 aircraft, accumulation upper bounds 99/405; capacity 2.3 aircraft/s.
quantitative_findings.conditions: Fixed simulated network identification and controller settings, not empirical flight measurements.

author_limitations.limitation: Objective-function weight calibration is difficult for a larger number of regions; current weights match the tested simulation settings and need further calibration for different scenarios.
Controller performance is evaluated with a specific demand distribution; different distributions across regions need testing.
MPC should be compared with other control methods for the combined departure/boundary problem.

Only one aircraft-command actuation approach with a specific random queuing setup is demonstrated, and the case study has limited airspace structure; other actuation methods and airspace structures need investigation.

Hovering at buffers may introduce conflicts and increased battery use; energy consumption is stated to be under separate ongoing investigation. Behavioral value of time, waiting/moving tradeoffs and schedule delays may inform future weights.

author_limitations.limitation: Departure-queue equation simplification assumes airports/vertiports saturated or oversaturated during rush hours; a more general conservation model could be substituted.

documents.title: Traffic flow modeling and feedback control for future Low-Altitude Air city Transport: An MFD-based approach
documents.metadata_verification: Title, authors, journal, volume, article number and DOI verified on PDF p.1; available online 17 November 2021.

method.mfd_source: Separate microscopic simulations follow Xue and Do 2019: double-integrator aircraft share future trajectories over a look-ahead horizon; coordinated maneuvers minimize deviation, solved as nonlinear integer programming with BARON. Generalized Edie variables are aggregated over 30 s, then averaged over each stationary-loading run into one MFD point (pp.5-6, Section 2.1).
method.structural_model: Proposes L fixed vertical layers, each partitioned into virtual regions with conditional borders and groups of individual virtual horizontal/interlayer gateways. Aircraft conservation with direction-specific accumulations produces a multi-region/layer MFD model. Gateway commands multiply nonlinear flow weighting factors and regional MFDs; demand is an uncontrolled disturbance (pp.6-8, Sections 2.2-3.1, Equations 1-5).
method.control: Partially linearized local dynamics retain nonlinear interregional terms, state delays and known input delays; unknown parameters/demand are covered by assumptions A1-A4. Continuous decentralized adaptive state-feedback MRAC is implemented with event-driven sample-and-hold of local gateway commands. Detector rule compares present, last-held and delayed inputs against fixed thresholds; event times are not a fixed control period (pp.9-12, Equations 6-17).
method.feedback_path: Local regional states/tracking errors and stable reference-model states enter decentralized controllers. Signals traverse delayed actuation channels to aggregate regional dynamics. State-delay terms also represent communication uncertainty. Theorem 1 guarantees bounded closed-loop signals/asymptotic tracking under A1-A4; appendix establishes a positive interevent-time lower bound (pp.9-12, Fig.5, Theorem 1; pp.16-18 Appendix/Remark 5).
method.macro_to_micro_scope: Section 3 represents control as commands of individual virtual traffic gateways. Section 5 evaluates the aggregated partially linearized three-region model (18). It does not present an aircraft-by-aircraft command conversion algorithm comparable to B12 Algorithms 2-3. The microscopic simulation in Section 2.1 is used to extract MFD, not the closed-loop control-test plant (pp.5-6,8,12-15).
method.queue_delay_accounting: For MFD extraction an aircraft unable to lift off safely hovers outside the square and chooses another lift-off time several seconds later. Section 5 reports regional tracking errors, control signals, demands and aggregated disturbance signals; it supplies no TTS/ground-vs-air queue comparison in that experiment. 'Delay' in control equations refers to input/state/communication delays and must not be mistaken for measured passenger/aircraft waiting delay (pp.6,9-15).
method.energy: Energy consumption is mentioned as an operational motivation (p.2), while the mathematical control/test model contains no battery/SOC state or energy objective (pp.8-15); this is observed formulation scope, not an author-declared limitation.
method.safety: MFD-generation microscopic model preserves a 15 m well-clear distance, 30 s lookahead, safe lift-off admission, coordinated conflict resolution. Aggregate control theorem concerns signal boundedness/tracking under model assumptions; it is not a separate individual-aircraft separation theorem (pp.5-6,11-12).

scenario.mfd_generation: 100 m-edge square; origins/destinations on different edges; 15 m well-clear distance; lookahead 30 s; speed <=20 m/s; acceleration <=5 m/s^2. Each constant-inflow run lasts 30 min, flow up to 65 aircraft/min. One case-study MFD is published (p.6).
scenario.control_test: Three aggregate regions, two in first layer and one in second. G1(n)=(vf1*n/A1)exp[-(1/a1)(n/ncr1)^a1], G2=0.8 G1, G3=1.2 G1; ncr1=80 aircraft, a1=0.73; normalized MFD and time-scaled partially linearized dynamics about n0=0.85 ncr. Parameters/disturbances unknown to controller; same controller/reference settings used without retuning across tested threshold cases (pp.12-14, Figs.6-7/Remark 4).
scenario.control_timing: Event driven, local sample/hold with fixed detector thresholds; no universal fixed sampling interval claimed. Simulation input delays h12=3,h13=0.1,h21=3,h23=0.2,h31=1,h32=0.7 after normalization/time scaling (pp.10,13).
scenario.disturbances: Bounded time-varying square-wave demands with offsets (0.13,0.2,0.3), amplitudes (-0.1,0.1,0.13), frequencies (0.29,0.25,0.21) in normalized/scaled test; r=(1,1.2,1.3), Ar=-1. Two detector-threshold parameter sets are compared (pp.13,15).

findings.claim: Simulation supports an MFD connecting trip completion and aircraft accumulation; safety-driven slowing/rerouting can lead to a congested branch. The published MFD uses stationary loading rather than transient-demand hysteresis tests.

A multi-layer, multi-region aggregate model and decentralized event-driven adaptive boundary control are developed; formal results address uncertain interconnections and delayed signals under assumptions A1-A4.
The numerical control demonstration concerns tracking errors/control/demand/disturbance histories for three aggregate regions under two threshold sets, with no retuning between tested cases.

quantitative_findings.result: ncr1=80 aircraft; G2=0.8G1 and G3=1.2G1; MFD shape exponent a1=0.73; operation point 0.85 ncr.
quantitative_findings.conditions: Chosen parameters for the three-region aggregate simulation, not measured critical accumulations for three real airspaces.

quantitative_findings.result: MFD construction covers stationary inflows up to 65 aircraft/min over 30-min runs, with 30-s aggregation before run averaging.
quantitative_findings.conditions: 100 m square, 15 m well clear, 20 m/s maximum speed, 5 m/s^2 acceleration, 30-s lookahead.

quantitative_findings.result: Theorem 1: all closed-loop signals bounded and tracking errors approach zero asymptotically; Appendix Remark 5 derives positive lower bound on interevent times (avoids Zeno behavior).
quantitative_findings.conditions: Mathematical result under Equations 6,11 and assumptions A1-A4, not a numerical percentage improvement.

author_limitations.limitation: Only one MFD-extraction case study is presented, derived from different stationary network loadings; different drone/operational parameters and microscopic control algorithms require investigation.
Dynamic loading with time-dependent demand and MFD hysteresis are future/ongoing work.
Inflow supply functions and capacity sharing among upstream regions are future modeling additions.
Physical meaning and analytical relationships for accumulation-dependent input delays h_i(n_i) and MFD require future investigation.

Alternative event-detector rules (relative, adaptive, switching thresholds) should be investigated/compared; current synthesis restricts attention to state-feedback Lyapunov design, while output-feedback variants are discussed as possible extensions.

evidence_locations: pp.5-6 microscopic MFD construction and Fig.3
pp.6-8 fixed multilayer/region/gateway design and nonlinear conservation dynamics
pp.9-12 delayed/event-driven MRAC, Fig.5, assumptions and theorem

old_claim_corrections.old: ABSTRACT_ONLY; three-region scenario and MFD parameters incompletely verified.
old_claim_corrections.correction: Full publisher PDF confirms 3 aggregate regions over 2 layers, exact chosen MFD and normalized test parameters, and threshold comparison.

old_claim_corrections.old: Adaptive boundary feedback robust to devices/communication anomalies.
old_claim_corrections.correction: Formal scope is delayed uncertain aggregate dynamics with assumptions A1-A4 and virtual-gateway actuation. Section 5 is not an integrated micro aircraft closed-loop simulation and does not numerically test every possible device/cyber fault.

root_judgment_items: Do not conflate input/state communication delays with TTS or actual waiting delay.
Do not conflate separate microscopic MFD identification and aggregate MRAC testing with B12's demonstrated command-subsystem feedback loop.

documents.title: Macroscopic Fundamental Diagrams for Low-Altitude Air city Transport
documents.metadata_verification: Title, authors, DOI, journal, volume and article number verified on p.1; available online 17 May 2023.

method.microscopic: Adapts Quan et al.'s distributed APF/Lyapunov-like collision avoidance. Position-velocity dynamics obey p_dot=v and v_dot=-L(v-vc); filtered position xi=p+L^-1 v converts motion into a single-integrator form. Velocity command combines an integral Lyapunov attraction term and barrier repulsion with saturation. Waypoint and destination-plane controllers are both implemented, including extension of destination lines to 3D planes (pp.3-7, Equations 1-23).
method.assumptions_and_safety: All aircraft fully controllable VTOL multicopters, capable of hovering; avoidance radius > safety radius and sufficient detection range (Assumption 1); static waypoint separation >= sum of avoidance radii (Assumption 2); initial filtered-position separation > sum of safety radii (Assumption 3); goal arrival/exit criteria (Assumptions 4/5). Safety and avoidance spaces are centered on filtered positions, detection sphere on actual position. Claimed conflict-free and convergence properties rely on these conditions and referenced proofs (pp.2,4-7).
method.mfd: Generalized Edie definitions extend to 2D/3D; sums of traveled distance/time over fixed spatial domain and aggregation window yield flow/density/speed. Trip completion is separately G=Nexit/Delta_tMFD. Simulation-step integration adapts aggregation when an aircraft is present for only part of a window. Exponential G(N) curves are fitted to simulation output (pp.7-8 Equations 24-30; pp.12,18 Tables 1-2).
method.feedback_and_control_scope: Microscopic positions/filtered positions drive local APF control every simulation step and trajectories feed synchronized macro-variable estimation. This paper identifies MFDs; it does not feed an MFD-based network controller back into departure/boundary actuators. Such control is explicitly future work. Simulation Algorithm 3 nevertheless has a safety-admission queue: if departure origin is within summed safety radii of an active aircraft, actual departure is postponed by Headway and status becomes Queued (pp.8-10,20,22-24).
method.time_scales: Simulation 0.5 s and MFD aggregation 60 s; 1.5 h default runs, 0.5 h for 3D example. Dynamic trapezoidal inflows include loading/unloading, enabling hysteresis analysis (p.10, Fig.6; pp.11-12).
method.configuration: Fixed geometry per run, no airways/intersections and free multidirectional routes. Independent case studies change network sizes, radii, heterogeneity, controller type and 2D/3D dimensionality; this is scenario comparison rather than dynamic reconfiguration of region boundaries (pp.9-11,14-16).
method.queue_delay_energy_scope: Appendix includes safety-induced departure queuing and planned/actual departure/arrival fields; reported experiments emphasize MFD curves, not TTS or battery/SOC accounting. No energy state/cost occurs in the presented plant/controller formulas. This is observed scope rather than a specific author limitation (pp.4-8,10-20,22-24).

scenario.default: Unstructured boundary-to-boundary uniformly random OD, default vmax=20 m/s, amax=5 m/s^2, rs=15 m, ra=22.5 m, rd=45.5 m. Simulation implemented in MATLAB R2021b on 2.8 GHz Intel i7/32 GB RAM (pp.8-10).
six_examples: Example 1: 2x2 km 2D waypoint network, peak inflow 0.2..2.1 aircraft/s (pp.10-12).
Example 2: 2x2,1x1,0.5x0.5 km networks with all other aircraft settings unchanged; different peak-inflow sweeps (p.13).
Example 3: rs=10,15,20 m, corresponding avoidance/detection radii; peak inflow sweeps 0.5..3.5,0.2..2.1,0.1..1.3 aircraft/s respectively (pp.13-14).
Example 4: 0.5x0.5 km heterogeneous traffic; rs uniform [10,20] m and/or vmax uniform [10,30] m/s, independent draws per aircraft/scenario; peak inflow 0.1..1.5 aircraft/s (pp.10,14-16).
Example 5: same 0.5x0.5 km, rs15/vmax20, waypoint versus destination-line approaches; peak inflow 0.1..1.2 aircraft/s (pp.14-18).
Example 6: 0.5x0.5x0.1 km 3D waypoint flight, 1800 s; prose peak inflow 0.1..1.0 aircraft/s, figure captions list 120,240,...,3600 aircraft/h (pp.11,16,19-20).

findings.claim: Full unimodal MFD shapes with congested branches arise across tested sizes, safety radii, aircraft heterogeneity, control algorithms and 2D/3D settings. Increasing safety radius lowers critical density and capacity; heterogeneous radius/speed increases Speed-MFD scatter.

Dynamic loading shows hysteresis: local congestion spots reduce mean speed/flow and may dissipate without complete network gridlock. Three-dimensional travel has more possible paths and greater scatter around critical state, with congestion appearing/dissolving more frequently; tested high-accumulation 3D cases need not gridlock.
Destination-line capacity exceeds waypoint capacity because destination lines relax the requirement to arrive at a particular point.
At gridlock, absolute flow Q may remain nonzero because aircraft continue local avoidance/search movement, while trip completion outflow G reaches zero. Therefore Q and G should not be equated.
Normalized flow-density curves do not coincide perfectly across sizes: N1/N2 show two congestion spots whereas smaller N3 shows one, according to the authors' inspection of simulation videos.

quantitative_findings.result: Example 1 observed critical point (229 aircraft,1.8667 aircraft/s), while the fitted curve peak is (283.86 aircraft,1.47 aircraft/s).

quantitative_findings.result: Peak inflow below 1.5 aircraft/s gives free flow with dissipating instantaneous congestion; at 1.6 aircraft/s a hysteresis loop occurs; above 1.8 aircraft/s the reported network gridlocks.
quantitative_findings.conditions: Example 1's dynamic trapezoidal demand/2x2 km network; exact prose says 'above 1.8' and Fig.8(c) shows 1.8.

Advanced MFD-based network control concepts/strategies are future work using this simulation environment and estimated MFDs.

documents.title: Urban low-altitude air transport management: Bridging dynamic traffic control and static network equilibrium
documents.metadata_verification: Title, authors, journal, volume, article number and DOI verified p.1; available online 26 June 2025.

method.static_planning: Aggregates UAM trips by OD, takeoff vertiport and landing vertiport. Travel cost includes constant accessing/cruising/egressing time and flow-dependent takeoff/landing waiting time. Elastic demand SO assignment minimizes travel cost minus inverse-demand integral, subject to flow conservation/nonnegativity; SO link flows are aggregated to regional endogenous/exogenous demand (pp.6-8, Equations 1-5). Network planning here means optimizing flows on a given network, not constructing/reconfiguring topology (p.2 footnote 2).
method.dynamic_models: Regional point queues satisfy Qdot=g-q with q=s*v, v in [0,1] and bounded queue lengths. Four regional accumulations satisfy MFD-based conservation. Modified Boundary Control (MBC) couples endogenous/exogenous outflow shares ui,i+ui,j=1, so aggregate G(n) is not reduced by metering. This differs from controlling only cross-boundary transfer (pp.8-10, Equations 6-11).
method.planning_control_connection: Derives s*=SO regional demand and chooses desired accumulation by the increasing/free-flow inverse MFD at sums of internal+cross demand. A maximum-throughput queue controller bounds admitted flow; MBC uij=min(qij/Gi(ni),1), uii=1-uij regulates the aggregate model. Equilibrium is updated when the assumed steady-state demand pattern changes. Proposition 2 proves convergence for oversaturated demand from an uncongested initial state (pp.10-13, Equations 12-20/Algorithm 1; Appendix C pp.22-23).
method.mfd_source: Uses prior microscopic simulation (Weng et al.2024) integrating collision avoidance/route guidance, calculates macroscopic variables from collision-free trajectories, fits flow-density data in a 1x1x1 km cube, then scales critical/jam accumulation by four for 2x2x1 km regions. Fitted alpha=.016,beta=1.136,Kcr=27.6,Kjam=200; case-study ncr=110.4,njam=800 (pp.13-14,Fig.8). The main planning/control experiments evolve aggregate equations (6),(10), not a live micro plant in Algorithm 1.
method.macro_to_micro: Section 2.3.2 proposes customized speed/route guidance to manipulate relative endogenous/exogenous outflow. Appendix A supplies a separate microscopic experiment showing the direction of flow response to differential speed limits. The detailed MBC mechanism is explicitly future work; Appendix A concludes conditionally that if MBC uij can be mapped to speed limit vmij, microscopic implementation becomes possible (p.10; pp.20-21).
method.actual_feedback: Main controller uses regional accumulation ni in Gi(ni), current admitted queue outflow qij and current demand/queue length. Algorithm 1 updates the queue and accumulation via model equations and recomputes SO when the steady-state demand function changes. The Appendix A test observes completion flows after an imposed speed switch; it is not presented as an implemented closed-loop uij-to-speed mapping (pp.12-13 Algorithm 1; pp.20-21).
method.time_scales: Two timescales: piecewise stable within-day patterns and short-term dynamic control. Numerical examples concatenate 0..60 and 60..120 min patterns; desired equilibrium updated at pattern change. A precise numerical integration/control sampling interval is not specified in the read main setup/Algorithm 1. Appendix A uses 0..450 and 450..900 s speed phases and examines transition 450..600 s (pp.6,10,13,15,17,20-21).
method.safety_and_energy_scope: Assumption 3 gives each aircraft sufficient mobility/intelligence to avoid collisions and stay within region during cruise; main equations impose aggregate free-flow/jam constraints rather than individual separation. Appendix A uses safety radius 50 m/detection 200 m in a collision-avoidance simulator. No battery/SOC state or energy objective in models/experiments (p.5 Assumption 3; pp.6-13; p.20).
method.queue_costs: Static takeoff/landing waits grow with vertiport flow; main dynamic queues represent admission demand on the ground aggregated across vertiports, with separate endogenous/exogenous subqueues. Remark 2 discusses balancing subqueue lengths and two independent takeoff platforms or boarding management for separation. It does not define B12-style aerial buffer queues (pp.6-8).

scenario.network: Cross-sea/river conceptual two-region system, full-mix airspace and fixed vertiport positions. Aircraft cross regions only during cruise. Eight vertiports and four OD pairs; two airspace regions each 2x2x1 km. No dynamic change of region topology is tested (pp.4-5,13-14).
scenario.assumptions: Central control can monitor/control individual passengers' vertiport selection and aircraft trajectories when needed; each vertiport supports simultaneous independent takeoff/landing; aircraft have collision-avoidance/stay-in-region ability; demand decomposes into periodically constant stable patterns (pp.5-6).

findings.claim: Proposed variable SO target adjusts the allowed admission rate and desired free-flow accumulation to a changed demand pattern. Maximum-throughput demand management filters demand noise when the queue is active; the stated MBC converges under Proposition 2 conditions.

Workday-to-holiday variable target admits more demand/reduces queues compared with fixed-workday SO baseline. Reverse switch lowers the desired state and capacity benchmark; fixed holiday target becomes unreachable under lower workday demand and queue management becomes inactive, allowing demand noise through.

Appendix A demonstrates a correlation between changed individual speed limits and regional completion-flow splits: endogenous completion flow falls and exogenous completion flow rises during450..600 s after the speed switch. This is evidence of microscopic controllability potential, not a completed quantitative MBC-to-speed mapping.

author_limitations.limitation: Detailed microscopic mechanism of MBC is left for future work; speed-control/route-guidance implementation is proposed and illustrated experimentally.
Independent takeoff/landing assumption disregards interaction between these operations; advanced collision-avoidance capabilities are assumed to permit system-level management.
Demand is simplified as a sequence of stable/periodically constant patterns.

Static planning treats access/cruise/egress time as constant and overlooks congestion-induced cruising-time increases; authors state admitted planning demand is guaranteed not to produce congestion and waits dominate cruising increase.
Proposed simple MBC guarantees convergence for oversaturated demand with initially uncongested states; advanced controllers such as MPC could improve transient performance.
